accroche: As long as no word exists to name it, an experience shared by thousands of people cannot be told, only endured in silence.
contenu_vulgarise:
A woman reacts badly to a supervisor's persistent and unwelcome advances. The people around her call her “humorless” or “too sensitive.” She herself finds no better way to describe what is happening to her, for lack of a word that would name it precisely. That word, sexual harassment, does not yet exist in everyday language: as long as it is missing, the experience remains real, but it cannot be told in terms that would make it recognized as a wrong.

## Two wrongs, not one

The British philosopher Miranda Fricker names this kind of situation in 2007, in *Epistemic Injustice: Power and the Ethics of Knowing* (Oxford University Press). She distinguishes two specifically epistemic wrongs there, meaning wrongs that strike a person precisely in their capacity to know and to make known, not in their income or their rights.

The first, testimonial injustice, occurs when a prejudice tied to a person's social identity, their gender, skin color, or accent, leads others to give less credit to what they report, regardless of the real quality of their testimony. A witness believed less because they belong to a certain group suffers a wrong that concerns nothing but their word: the facts they report can be perfectly accurate, the wrong is already done the moment they are heard with less attention.

The second, hermeneutical injustice, is harder to spot, since the person concerned does not even have the words to describe what is happening to them. The interpretive resources available in a society at a given moment leave certain experiences in the dark, most often those of groups that took no part in the collective shaping of shared meaning. That is exactly the situation of a woman facing advances at work before the concept of sexual harassment was available to name it: she is not missing vocabulary by accident, she is missing a category that no one, in the shared construction of language, had previously had any reason to build.

## What this shifts

The shift lies in applying the word “epistemic” to injustice: injustice is usually filed under distribution, income, rights, positions, never under knowledge itself. Fricker shows that a person can be wronged in their capacity to know and to make known, independently of any material inequality besides. Hermeneutical injustice has a consequence of its own, beyond the case that gave it its most cited example: once a word exists for an experience, that experience changes status, it becomes tellable, comparable from one testimony to another, and eventually recognized by an institution. Naming is therefore not an optional extra to justice, it is one of its conditions.

repere.texte: Before the concept of sexual harassment became available, women facing persistent unwanted advances at work were judged by those around them as “humorless” or “too sensitive,” with no word available to name precisely what was happening to them. The philosopher Miranda Fricker takes up this example in Epistemic Injustice (2007) to define hermeneutical injustice: the wrong suffered by someone who lacks the interpretive resources needed to make their own experience understood.
repere.source: Miranda Fricker, Epistemic Injustice: Power and the Ethics of Knowing, Oxford University Press, 2007; example taken up by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Feminist Epistemology and Philosophy of Science,” 2024

carte.punch: As long as no word exists to name it, an experience cannot be told, only endured in silence.
carte.idee: In 2007, philosopher Miranda Fricker named epistemic injustice: being believed less because of a prejudice (testimonial injustice), or lacking the words to make what you live through understood (hermeneutical injustice), like harassment before that word existed.

quiz.question: What distinguishes hermeneutical injustice from testimonial injustice, according to Miranda Fricker?
choix: Hermeneutical injustice only affects witnesses in a courtroom
In hermeneutical injustice, the person lacks the words to describe what they live through
Hermeneutical injustice is a form of economic injustice, not epistemic
Hermeneutical injustice only concerns experts and scientists
quiz.explication: Hermeneutical injustice is not limited to courtrooms or experts, and it remains epistemic in nature, not economic. What sets it apart from testimonial injustice, where a person is believed less because of a prejudice, is that here the interpretive resources needed to name the experience are simply missing.
